steps.title: Hold hollandaise through service
steps.prompt: Put the stages of holding a batch of hollandaise through service in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Take the yolks from the fridge for a small batch timed to service, and note the time: the sauce's clock starts there
Make the hollandaise, then strain it into a clean, dry container, never one that held the last batch
Label it the moment it is filled, with the time it was made and the time it must be gone, then stand it in a bain-marie that steams but never bubbles, away from the flame
Through service, stir it now and then so no skin forms, and check it with a probe thermometer
Discard it when its time runs out, or sooner if it splits, skins or smells sour, and start the next batch clean
steps.distractor: Pour the fresh batch onto what is left of the old sauce, so nothing goes to waste
steps.why: The clock starts when the yolks leave the fridge, not when the sauce is finished, and sets the label. Where it sits below 57°C (135°F), the sauce runs on the kitchen's written time limit. Old sauce is never topped up: the new batch would take on its time and whatever has grown in it.

steps.title: Cool a stock in two stages
steps.prompt: Put the stages of cooling a large batch of stock in order, from the stove to the walk-in. One stage does not belong.
steps: Take the stock off the stove and start cooling at once, never leaving it on the range
Strain the stock off its bones and vegetables, dividing it among smaller metal containers
Stand them in an ice bath, with ice and water up to the level of the stock
Stir the stock often, or stir an ice wand through it, topping up the ice as it melts
Probe the centre of each and log it: down to 21°C (70°F) within 2 hours
Once it has reached 21°C (70°F), label each container and set it on a top shelf of the walk-in, loosely covered, with nothing stacked on it
Probe and log again: 5°C (41°F) or below within 6 hours of the start
steps.distractor: Put the full stockpot straight into the walk-in with a tight lid on
steps.why: Straining takes out the bones and vegetables that hold heat; the batch is divided and set in ice at once, and stirring carries heat to the cold wall. The first stage, to 21°C (70°F) within 2 hours, has the shorter clock because bacteria grow quickest there. A hot pot in the walk-in warms everything around it.

steps.title: Take an allergy to the kitchen
steps.prompt: A guest tells you of a food allergy: put the server's routine in order, from the table to the kitchen and back. One stage does not belong.
steps: Listen while the guest says it in full, neither arguing nor reassuring
Write it on the ticket, against the right seat
Tell the chef, or whoever runs the pass, in person as well as through the printer
Bring the chef's answer back to the guest in the chef's words
When the plate is up, carry it by itself, straight from the pass
Name the dish as it lands in front of the guest
steps.distractor: Tell the guest the dish should be fine, since the menu does not list it
steps.why: The guest is heard in full and the need is written against the seat, then said to the chef face to face, because a printed ticket can be missed in a rush. Only the chef's answer goes back to the table, and the plate travels alone so nothing touches it on the way.

match.title: Safety cue to action
match.prompt: Match each cue on the line or the floor to what a trained hand does next.
pairs: The thermometer was knocked or dropped
Calibrate it in iced water before it is used again
An oyster gapes and will not close when tapped
Throw it out: it is dead
The flambé flame grows too big or spreads
Slide the lid over the pan and turn the burner off
A guest names a food allergy
Tell the kitchen in person, as well as on the ticket
The ice bath under the stock has turned to warm water
Drain some water, add fresh ice and keep stirring
A fresh batch of hollandaise is ready and old sauce remains
Start a new labelled container; never top up the old
A guest asks whether a runny yolk is all right to eat
Point to the menu's advisory and offer to ask the kitchen
Frozen shrimp are wanted for tomorrow's service
Thaw them in the walk-in overnight

match.title: Temperatures that matter
match.prompt: Match each temperature from the FDA Food Code to what it marks in the kitchen.
pairs: Cold holding, and the end of cooling within 6 hours
Raw shell eggs: the storage air at or below it
The first stage of cooling, reached within 2 hours
Hot holding: food kept at or above it
Fish, whole cuts of meat and an egg broken to order, held 15 seconds
Poultry, stuffed foods, and cooled food reheated for hot holding
